title.en: The Serpent That Called the Reef to Rise

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In the beginning nothing existed but a wide sea, and in it swam a great serpent. Wanting a resting place, the serpent called out, 'Let the reef rise!' — and the reef rose from the ocean and became dry land.
summary.zh: 太初唯有一片汪洋，巨蛇游於其中。蛇欲得一棲息之所，便呼曰『礁石升起吧！』——礁石遂自海中浮出，化為陸地。

sensitivity.note: Recorded by a museum anthropologist (Dixon 1916) from Admiralty Islands informants; colonial-era collection, heritage held by Manus communities.

passages.text: A part of the people of the Admiralty Islands believed that once there was nothing in the world but a wide-spread sea. In this primeval ocean swam a great serpent, and because the serpent had no place on which he might rest, he called out, 'Let the reef rise!' And the reef rose up out of the ocean and became dry land. In this way the first solid ground in the world came into being — the serpent's own words lifting the foundation of the islands out of the endless water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Couple on the Driftwood

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A variant Admiralty Islands creation story: a man and a woman floated on the primeval sea on a piece of driftwood, watching to see whether the ocean would dry up. When the waters retired they planted trees and created the food plants on the barren new land.
summary.zh: 阿德米羅提群島另一創世異文：一男一女乘浮木漂流於太初之海，觀察海水是否退去。水退陸現，惟大地荒蕪無物，二人遂種樹、造百種食物。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); heritage held by Manus communities.

passages.text: Another Admiralty Islands version differs from the serpent's reef: a man and a woman, after having floated upon the primeval sea, climbed upon a piece of driftwood and wondered whether the ocean would ever dry up. At last the waters wholly retired, and land appeared, covered with hills — but barren and without life. Whereupon the two beings planted trees and created foods of various sorts, stocking the empty world with forest and garden from their driftwood vantage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu Fish Up the Land
title.zh: 托卡比納那與托卡武武釣起陸地

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: On New Britain the familiar Polynesian-style myth of fishing land from the bottom of the sea is told of the culture-hero brothers To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu, who haul up islands from the deep for their people.
summary.zh: 新不列顛島流傳與波利尼西亞相仿的『釣起陸地』神話：文化英雄兄弟托卡比納那與托卡武武自深海拉起島嶼，為其子民造地。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage of the Gazelle Peninsula.

passages.text: Among the coastal tribes of the Gazelle Peninsula of New Britain we find the familiar story of the fishing of the land from the bottom of the sea, a task accomplished by the two culture-hero brothers, To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu. The wise elder brother drew the land upward from the deep, and the islands of their coasts rose where he pulled; the fool of a younger brother lent his hand to the same work, his blunders marking the imperfections of the new earth. Some of their other deeds — the making of the first women, the carved shark, the roasted mother — fill the rest of the Gazelle cycle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Fishing Up the Land in the Southern New Hebrides
title.zh: 新赫布里底群島南部的釣地神話

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島南部（塔納—埃羅芒加）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The same conception of land fished up from the bottom of the sea, told in slightly greater detail, is found in the southern New Hebrides — the southernmost reach of the tale, far from its New Britain home.
summary.zh: 『自海底釣起陸地』之說亦見於新赫布里底群島南部，敘述稍詳——此乃該神話分布之最南端，遠離其新不列顛故地。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); heritage of southern Vanuatu communities.

passages.text: Dixon notes that the story of the fishing of the land from the bottom of the sea, told on New Britain by To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu, is found also in the southern New Hebrides in slightly greater detail. There the first dry ground of the islands was likewise drawn up from the deep — a striking instance of one tale-idea travelling the full length of the Melanesian chain, from the Bismarck Archipelago to the islands that lie nearly opposite New Caledonia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Manual Carves a Wife from Wood

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Manual, alone in the Admiralty Islands, longed for a wife. He felled a tree, shaped the trunk into a woman's figure, and spoke: 'My wood there, become a woman!' — and the image came to life.
summary.zh: 阿德米羅提群島的曼努爾獨居渴偶。他入林伐木，將樹幹雕成女子之形，念咒曰：『我的木頭啊，成為女人吧！』木像遂活。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Manus heritage. Motif 'clay-humans' used for its making-by-speech parallel.

passages.text: In the Admiralty Islands it is said that Manual was alone and longed for a wife. So he took his axe, went into the forest, and cut down a tree, and after he had fashioned the trunk into the figure of a woman, he spoke to it: 'My wood there, become a woman!' And the image came to life — the first marriage of mankind made not by finding a bride but by carving one, the carver's speech turning wood into flesh.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Qat Carves the First Six Humans

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Qat, the first maker of men, cut wood of the dracaena tree into six figures — three men and three women — hid them three days, then danced and drummed before them until they stirred and stood alive; he joined them into three married pairs.
summary.zh: 卡特首造人類：以龍血樹之木刻成六像，三男三女；藏之三日，取出立起，於其前跳舞擊鼓，木像漸動而得自立——『如是誘之入生』；遂配為三對夫妻。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref qat-creation (same episode in Codrington).

passages.text: In the Banks Islands, Qat was the first to make man, cutting wood out of the dracaena-tree and forming it into six figures, three men and three women. When he had finished them, he hid them away for three days, after which he brought them forth and set them up. Dancing in front of them and seeing that they began to move, he beat the drum before them, and they moved still more, and thus he beguiled them into life, so that they could stand of themselves. Then he divided them into three pairs as man and wife — the first marriages of the Banks Islands made by Qat's own hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: Marawa Buries His People: The Origin of Death
title.zh: 馬拉瓦埋活人：死亡之起源

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Marawa, envious of Qat, copied his wooden figures and drummed them alive; then he buried his people seven days in a pit lined with coconut fronds — and dug them up lifeless and decomposed. So death came among men.
summary.zh: 馬拉瓦嫉妒卡特，仿其法刻木鼓而活之；卻將其所造之人埋入鋪椰葉之坑七日——掘出時已死而腐。人類之死，由此而始。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref qat-creation.

passages.text: Now Marawa, who was a malicious, envious fellow, saw what Qat had made and determined to do likewise. So he took wood of another sort, and when he had fashioned the images, he set them up and beat the drum before them, and gave them life as Qat had done. But when he saw them move, he dug a pit and covered the bottom with coco-nut fronds, burying his men and women in it for seven days; and when he dug them up again, he found them lifeless and decomposed. This was the origin of death among men — mortality entering the world through the envy of the copyist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: The Clay Man and the Twig Woman

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In another Banks Islands version, Qat made the first man of red clay, and the first woman of supple rods and rings covered with the spathes of sago palms — exactly as the people themselves make the tall dance-hats of the sacred ceremonies.
summary.zh: 班克斯群島另一異文：卡特以紅土造首男，以柔枝與環、外覆西米棕櫚葉鞘造首女——正如島民製作聖舞高帽之法。

passages.text: According to another version from the same Banks Islands area, while the first man was made of red clay by Qat, he created the first woman of rods and rings of supple twigs covered with the spathes of sago palms — just as they make the tall hats which are used in the sacred dances. Man and woman of the first day were thus made of the two most ritual materials of the islands: the earth itself, and the ceremonial craft of the dance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: Takaro's Ten Mud Men and the First Woman
title.zh: 塔卡羅造十泥人與首位女子

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島（安巴埃島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Takaro made ten figures from mud and breathed life into them; unsatisfied with a world of men, he changed one into a woman with a thrown fruit, then sent each man to her for fire and water until the last she called husband.
summary.zh: 塔卡羅以泥塑十人像，吹氣使活；世間皆男，塔卡羅不滿，擲果一枚使其化為女子，令九男依次向她求火、求水，逐一被稱為兄長，唯末一人稱為夫。

passages.text: A tale of the creation of man from earth is told in the New Hebrides. Takaro made from mud ten figures of men. When they were finished, he breathed upon them — upon their eyes, their ears, their mouths, their hands, their feet — and thus the images became alive. But all the people he had made were men, and Takaro was not satisfied.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So he told them to light a fire and cook some food, then ordered them to stand still while he threw a fruit at one of them — and lo, one of the men was changed into a woman. Takaro sent the woman to dwell by herself in a house. One by one he sent the nine men to her, first to ask for fire, then for water; each she greeted as her elder brother, her younger brother, her kinsman — all but the last, and him she called her husband. So Takaro said to him, 'Take her as your wife, and you two shall live together.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Drawn in Blood: The Birth of the Two Brothers

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A being drew two figures of men on the ground, cut himself with a knife, sprinkled the drawings with his blood, and covered them with leaves; they came to life as To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu. The elder then threw two unripe coconuts to earth and two women burst from them.
summary.zh: 有神者於地上畫二男形，以刀自割，以其血灑畫，覆之以葉；畫遂活為托卡比納那與托卡武武。兄攀椰樹擲青椰二枚落地，爆裂而化為二女，娶之為妻。

passages.text: In the beginning, a being drew two figures of men upon the ground, and then, cutting himself with a knife, he sprinkled the two drawings with his blood and covered them over with leaves. The result was that they came to life as To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu, the wise and the foolish brother of the Gazelle Peninsula.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: To-Kabinana then climbed a coco-nut-tree which bore light yellow nuts, and picking two unripe ones, he threw them to the ground, where they burst and changed into two women, whom he took as his wives. His brother asked how he had come to be possessed of the two women, and To-Kabinana told him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: To-Karvuvu's Ugly-Nosed Wives

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: To-Karvuvu copied his brother's coconut trick, but his nuts fell on their under side and burst into two women with depressed, ugly noses. Jealous, he abandoned his own wives and took one of To-Kabinana's.
summary.zh: 托卡武武仿兄擲椰，然其椰以底觸地，爆出二女，鼻樑低塌貌醜。他嫉妒兄之美妻，遂棄己二妻，而奪托卡比納那之一妻。

passages.text: To-Karvuvu also climbed a tree and likewise threw down two nuts; but they fell so that their under side struck the ground, and from them came two women with depressed, ugly noses. So To-Karvuvu was jealous because his brother's wives were better looking than his, and he took one of To-Kabinana's spouses, abandoning the two ugly females who were his own — the foolish brother's first great blunder, and the tale's aition of why some families prosper and some do not.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Light and Dark Coconut Women

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: To-Kabinana tied a light-coloured coconut to his canoe and it became a handsome woman; the foolish brother's dark nut became a black-skinned woman. From the two descends mankind, divided into two classes, and with the dark woman death entered the world: 'if all of us were only light of skin, we should not die.'
summary.zh: 托卡比納那以白椰繫舟尾，化為俊美女子；弟之黑椰則化黑膚女子。兩類人由此而生：白皮者不致於死，黑椰女一脈則必死——托卡武武之愚遂為人類招致死亡與分化。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916). The tale encodes a local dual-marriage-class rule; recorded as ethnographic material, not endorsement.

passages.text: To-Kabinana said to To-Karvuvu, 'Do you get two light-coloured coco-nuts. One of them you must hide, then bring the other to me.' To-Karvuvu, however, did not obey, but got one light and one dark nut, and having hidden the latter, he brought the light-coloured one to his brother, who tied it to the stern of his canoe and paddled out to sea. Soon the coco-nut turned into a handsome woman, who sat on the stern of the canoe and steered while To-Kabinana paddled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When To-Karvuvu brought the other coco-nut, his brother saw that it was dark-coloured and upbraided him: 'You are indeed a stupid fellow. You have brought misery upon our mortal race.' They tied the dark nut to the stern and paddled away, and it turned into a black-skinned woman. Then To-Kabinana said: 'Alas, you have only ruined our mortal race. If all of us were only light of skin, we should not die. Now, however, this dark-skinned woman will produce one group, and the light-skinned woman another, and the light-skinned men shall marry the dark-skinned women, and the dark-skinned men shall marry the light-skinned women.' And so To-Kabinana divided mankind into two classes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dove's Son

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: One Admiralty Islands version of human origins: a dove bore two young, one of which was a bird and one a man, who became the ancestor of the human race by incestuous union with his mother.
summary.zh: 阿德米羅提群島人類起源之一說：一鳩產二雛，一為鳥，一為人；此人與其母鳩结合，遂為人類之祖。

passages.text: In the Admiralty Islands, according to one version, a dove bore two young, one of which was a bird and one a man. The man became the ancestor of the human race by incestuous union with his mother — the first people of the islands descending from a bird's brood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tortoise's Ten Eggs

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Another Admiralty Islands recension: a tortoise laid ten eggs, from which were hatched eight tortoises and two human beings, a man and a woman, who married and became the ancestors of both light-skinned and dark-skinned people.
summary.zh: 阿德米羅提群島另一異文：一龜產十卵，孵化得八龜與二人——一男一女；二人成婚，遂為白膚與黑膚人種之共祖。

passages.text: Another recension has it that a tortoise laid ten eggs, from which were hatched eight tortoises and two human beings, one man and one woman. These two, marrying, became the ancestors of both light-skinned and dark-skinned people — the human stock of the Admiralties hatched from a single clutch beside their tortoise siblings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Ndengei Hatches the First Pair

region.en: Viti Levu, Fiji (Nakauvadra range, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟維提島（納夸瓦德拉山，象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In Fiji, a bird laid two eggs which were hatched by Ndengei, the great serpent — a boy coming from one and a girl from the other. The serpent-god of the Nakauvadra cave thus brooded mankind into being.
summary.zh: 斐濟神話：一鳥產二卵，由巨蛇恩登蓋孵化——一卵出男，一卵出女。納夸瓦德拉山洞中之蛇神遂成孵育人類之祖。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); iTaukei heritage. Cross-ref thomson-fijians records.

passages.text: In Fiji it is said that a bird laid two eggs which were hatched by Ndengei, the great serpent — a boy coming from one and a girl from the other. Thus the first Fijians were brooded into life by the serpent who dwells in the earth, and Ndengei, the old stone-eating snake-god of the Nakauvadra, stands at the head of the race as its incubator rather than its maker.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: From the Egg a Worm, from the Worm a Man

region.zh: 托雷斯海峽東部群島（摩爾島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: According to the Eastern Islanders of Torres Strait, a bird having laid an egg, a maggot or worm was developed from it, which then was transformed into human shape.
summary.zh: 托雷斯海峽東部島民之說：一鳥產卵，卵中生出蛆蟲，蛆蟲再變化為人形。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Meriam heritage of Torres Strait.

passages.text: A variant of the egg-origin tale is found in Torres Straits where, according to the Eastern Islanders, a bird having laid an egg, a maggot or worm was developed from it, which then was transformed into human shape — life passing in three stages, from the bird's egg through the lowly worm to the first human form.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Hi-asa's Blood, Two Eggs

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The woman Hi-asa, living alone, cut her finger while shaving pandanus strips and caught the blood in a mussel-shell. After eleven days the blood held two eggs, which burst into a man and a woman — the parents of the human race.
summary.zh: 獨居女子希阿莎削露兜樹條時割傷手指，以蚌殼接血覆蓋之。十一日後血中化二卵，數日卵裂，出一男一女——人類之父母由此而生。

passages.text: One version from the Admiralty Islands tells of an origin of mankind from a clot of blood. A woman named Hi-asa, who lived alone, one day cut her finger while shaving pandanus strips. Collecting the blood from the wound in a mussel-shell, she put a cover over it and set it away; but when, after eleven days, she looked in the shell, it contained two eggs. She covered them up, and after several days they burst, one producing a man and the other a woman, who became the parents of the human race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Woman's Arms: Blood of the Pandanus

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: An old woman wading for shellfish scratched her aching arms with sharp pandanus strips and laid the blood-covered strips in a refuse heap. The pile swelled, and from the blood of her right arm grew To-Kabinana, from her left To-Karvuvu.
summary.zh: 一老嫗涉水拾貝，雙臂痠痛，以利露兜樹條先後割左右臂，將染血樹條棄於垃圾堆中。日後垃圾堆隆起，右臂之血生托卡比納那，左臂之血生托卡武武。

passages.text: While an old woman was wading in the sea searching for shellfish, her arms pained her, and so, taking two sharp strips of pandanus, she scratched and cut first one arm and then the other. The two strips of pandanus, thus covered with her blood, she laid away in a heap of refuse which she intended to burn; but after a time the pile began to swell, and when she was about to set fire to it, she saw that two boys had grown from her blood — from the blood of her right arm, To-Kabinana, and from that of her left arm, To-Karvuvu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sprouting Sugar-Cane

region.zh: 所羅門群島（象徵定位：瓜達爾卡納爾）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In the Solomon Islands, mankind came from plants: two knots began to sprout on a stalk of sugar-cane, and when the cane below each sprout burst, from one issued a man and from the other a woman — the parents of the race.
summary.zh: 所羅門群島之說：一節甘蔗生出兩個芽瘤，芽下之莖先後爆裂，一瘤出男、一瘤出女——人類之父母自此而生。

passages.text: An origin of the human race from plants seems definitely stated only in the Solomon Islands, where it is said that two knots began to sprout on a stalk of sugar-cane, and when the cane below each sprout burst, from one issued a man and from the other a woman — these becoming the parents of mankind. Humanity thus sprouting from the cane that still sweetens Solomon feasts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman in the Wild Cane

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Two men (some say To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu) netted a piece of wild sugar-cane three times and planted it. The planted cane swelled, burst, and a woman stepped out to cook their food secretly, until they caught and kept her.
summary.zh: 兩個男人（或謂托卡比納那與托卡武武）夜漁三網得一根野蔗，棄之不去，遂種之。蔗株日漸膨脹，一日爆裂，走出一名女子為他們暗備飯食；二人潛伏捉住她，其一娶之為妻，人類自此傳衍。

passages.text: Two men (sometimes described as To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu) were fishing at night, and while they were so engaged a piece of wild sugar-cane floated into the net, where it became entangled. Disengaging it, they threw it away, but again it was enmeshed and was once more discarded. When, however, it was caught for the third time, they determined to plant it, and did so. Taking root, the cane grew, and after a time it began to swell, until one day, while the two men were absent at work, the stalk burst and from it came out a woman who cooked food for the men and then returned to her hiding-place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The men came back from their work and were much surprised to find their food ready; and since the same thing occurred the next day, on the following morning they hid themselves to see who it was that had prepared their food. After a time the stalk opened and the woman came out, whereupon they immediately seized her and held her fast. In some versions, the woman then became the wife of one of the men, and all mankind are supposed to be descended from the pair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Woman from the Tree, Man from the Ground

region.en: Elema country, Gulf of Papua (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 巴布亞灣埃勒馬地區（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Among the Papuan Elema of British New Guinea, the first woman sprang from a tree and the first man from the ground.
summary.zh: 英屬新幾內亞埃勒馬巴布亞人之說：首位女子生於樹，首位男子生於地。

passages.text: Among the Papuan tribes of Elema in British New Guinea, an origin is given of the first woman from a tree and of the first man from the ground — the two first ancestors drawn from the forest and from the soil on which the tribe still plants its sago and taro.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cowrie-Shell Woman

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島（象徵定位：聖靈島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: In the New Hebrides, the first female being is said to have sprung from a cowrie-shell which turned into a woman.
summary.zh: 新赫布里底群島之說：第一位女性由一枚寶螺所化，螺殼開而成人形女子。

passages.text: In the New Hebrides the first female being is said to have sprung from a cowrie-shell which turned into a woman — the cowrie, prized across Melanesia as wealth and ornament for the bride-price, becoming in the story the very shell of womanhood itself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.
